README.md describes the directory tree only as a markdown code fence for humans, not as structured/parseable data. grep -rn for the actual git HEAD sha (d399fd6...) and for any 'HEAD'/'commit'-pin language across rewrite/*.md returns nothing relevant — legacy source citations are by file/function name only (e.g. 'ticketd/app/server.py::request_reset'), never pinned to a commit SHA. ticketd/.git HEAD is d399fd60ef97d50d6e6cfda2b2a28a1bb9ea5484 and nothing in the workspace records or matches it.

expectations.text: Legacy tree is protected against modification by at least one working mechanism (write permissions, commit guard, or git pin) — verified by attempting a write/commit
expectations.evidence: Directly tested: `touch outputs/ticketd/app/__grader_write_test__.py` succeeded (exit 0, file created writable). Also `cd outputs/ticketd && git add __grader_test.txt && git commit -m ...` succeeded outright (commit a007768 created, then reset back). No pre-commit hook, no read-only permissions, no git pin/lock of any kind protects the legacy tree — only a prose instruction ('The legacy app (ticketd/) is a read-only reference. Do not modify it.' in plans/00-project-setup.md) which is advisory text, not an enforced mechanism.

expectations.evidence: 01-CURRENT-BEHAVIOR-CONTRACT.md does use an explicit, consistently-applied 3-way taxonomy ([PRESERVE]/[PRESERVE-CRITICAL] / [FIX] / [OPEN]) which maps to 3 of the 4 requested categories, but has no 'mechanism-free' category at all (new-build elements like the outbox worker or verification scripts are never tagged as having no legacy analog). expectations.text: The 200-with-empty-body-for-missing-ticket quirk is captured as behavior to preserve, with citation to its code site
expectations.evidence: 01-CURRENT-BEHAVIOR-CONTRACT.md §2: 'GET /api/tickets/<int:id> — [PRESERVE-CRITICAL] — if no row matches, returns 200 {}, not 404. expectations.text: The synchronous-email defect is dispositioned as a sanctioned change (not faithful reproduction), linked to an expected-divergence/changelog entry so verification will pass the intentional fix
expectations.evidence: 01-CURRENT-BEHAVIOR-CONTRACT.md tags the close-endpoint's synchronous send_mail() as '[FIX — top priority]' (not preserve), and DESIGN-async-notifications.md documents the sanctioned outbox+poller replacement in detail. This is linked to a concrete verification mechanism: verification/VERIFICATION.md's acceptance-criteria table maps 'Closing tickets survives an SMTP outage' directly to verification/smtp_outage_test.py, a dedicated regression script (syntax-checked via py_compile) that asserts close-latency stays flat against an unreachable SMTP host — i.e. verification is explicitly built to expect and pass the new async behavior rather than flag it as a legacy-parity regression. (Note: parity_check.py's KNOWN_DIFFERENCES list, which is the file's mechanism for encoding intentional deviations, does not separately mention the async change — but that's because the close-endpoint's JSON response shape is unchanged, so no parity-diff entry was needed; the dedicated smtp_outage_test.py plus the acceptance table cover it.)

expectations.text: An ordered backlog and machine-readable ledger exist; the first milestone is a thin end-to-end walking skeleton; work orders declare dependencies
expectations.evidence: README.md has an ordered Phase table (0-6) with a 'Depends on' column, which is a real (if prose/markdown) dependency declaration — but there is no machine-readable ledger anywhere (no JSON/YAML backlog/ledger file; grep -rin for 'walking skeleton'/'thin slice'/'vertical slice' across the whole rewrite/ tree returns zero hits). Phase 0 (plans/00-project-setup.md) is pure scaffolding — dependency install, Docker Compose, Alembic wiring, a CI-equivalent check script — with no working end-to-end route/feature stood up and verified via a real request; it is not framed or built as a thin walking skeleton (one full vertical slice proven end-to-end before breadth work), just conventional phase-by-phase setup-then-features ordering.

expectations.text: A verification harness exists: replay/diff mechanism with normalization rules, expected divergences, and runnable twin-boot scripts (or an explicit, honest record of what could not be built)
expectations.evidence: A real replay/diff script exists (verification/parity_check.py, 5 concrete checks, syntax-verified with py_compile) and expected divergences are documented as a KNOWN_DIFFERENCES text block covering the priority-422 and slug-suffix intentional changes. However, two of the three named harness components are genuinely absent: (1) no normalization rules — grep for 'normaliz' in parity_check.py returns nothing; timestamp/whitespace/field normalization is not implemented anywhere in the diff logic, it's sidestepped by only checking key-sets rather than values in most checks; (2) no runnable twin-boot scripts — find for '*.sh' across outputs/ returns nothing; VERIFICATION.md instead gives manual copy-paste terminal commands ('# terminal 1... # terminal 2... # terminal 3'). The README does honestly disclose that the scripts were 'not run end-to-end... since that requires a running instance of the (not yet built) new API,' but never specifically flags the missing normalization logic or missing boot automation as gaps — so the fallback 'explicit, honest record of what could not be built' only partially covers what's actually missing.

claims.evidence: Re-ran `python3 -m py_compile rewrite/verification/parity_check.py rewrite/verification/smtp_outage_test.py` — compiles cleanly, confirming the claim.

claims.claim: The access log is a single-hour synthetic sample, not a real 30-day log
claims.evidence: 04-TRAFFIC-ANALYSIS.md shows the derivation commands and results (single date 12/Jul/2026, single 60-minute window, single client identity) — this is a well-evidenced and important catch that the eval prompt's '~30-day access log' framing was itself questionable, and the executor flagged it prominently rather than silently using bad data.

The tree was not modified by the executor, but it is trivially writable and committable by anyone/anything afterward (verified by direct write+commit test) — so 'untouched' describes what happened, not a guarantee that holds going forward, which is the actual failure mode assertion 2 is testing for.

uncertainties: No user_notes.md file exists in outputs/ — open questions/uncertainties are instead folded into 03-OPEN-QUESTIONS.md (8 items) and the final_report.md limitation note about the access log.

suggestions.assertion: Legacy tree is protected against modification by at least one working mechanism
suggestions.reason: This assertion is well-designed and discriminating — it correctly caught a real gap. The executor produced good prose instructions ('read-only reference, do not modify') but zero enforcement, and a trivial write+commit test proved the tree fully mutable. Worth keeping as-is; it cleanly separates 'said the right thing' from 'built the guarantee.'

No assertion checks whether the workspace's own internal cross-references are consistent/correct (e.g., README's phase-dependency table vs. what each plans/NN file actually declares, or whether DESIGN docs and the behavior contract ever contradict each other on a specific quirk). I did not find contradictions in this run, but a large hand-authored, cross-linked doc set like this is exactly where drift creeps in silently, and no assertion would currently catch it.

Assertion 9's phrase 'machine-readable ledger' and assertion 10's 'normalization rules'/'runnable twin-boot scripts' are precise and rightly demanding — they were the clearest fails in this run and are good discriminators between 'wrote thorough prose about it' and 'actually built the mechanism.' No change needed, just noting they did their job.

suggestions.assertion: Feature specs tag behaviors with an explicit fidelity taxonomy... and cite file:line evidence
suggestions.reason: Consider whether 'file:line' should be read strictly or whether an unambiguous file:function locator in a small, well-organized codebase (this one: 4 short source files) should count as equivalent evidence-resolution. I graded strictly per the literal wording (no line numbers appear anywhere in this workspace), but a grader with a looser reading could reasonably pass this given how easy the citations are to verify by hand. Worth the eval author deciding explicitly which reading is intended, since it changes this assertion's verdict.

eval_feedback.overall: 6 of 10 assertions failed, but not uniformly — this is a genuinely strong, thorough, honestly-caveated planning document set (the access-log-is-fake catch, the slug-collision non-decision, the sync-email disposition, and the 200-empty-object quirk preservation are all handled with real rigor). What it lacks is almost entirely infrastructure/tooling rather than judgment: no machine-readable manifest or ledger, no enforced write-protection on the legacy tree, no line-level citations, and a verification harness that's real but missing normalization and boot automation. That pattern — correct analysis, absent tooling — is exactly what a 'no skill' baseline run would be expected to produce versus a skill that scaffolds those mechanical artifacts by default.
